prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of prose and poetry in which memory, the body and metaphysical speculation are built into an expansive, densely patterned imaginative architecture.

statement.case_for: On public knowledge of the works, not on direct reading, Cărtărescu has the strongest claim on the common criteria. His voice is unmistakable. Blinding and Solenoid fuse memory, the body, dream and cosmological speculation into large, recursive prose structures. This is a formal and linguistic ambition sustained over decades, not a single peak, and it carries real imaginative and intellectual depth. The lyric origins in his poetry give the prose its rhythmic and imagistic texture, which supports a citation covering the whole oeuvre rather than one title. The recent large-scale books appear to extend the project rather than repeat it, though I cannot verify this independently. I reconsidered the opening ranking against the candidates my colleagues defend, and none of those arguments displaces him. Michon and Can Xue have the strongest competing claims on voice, Zurita and Carson on formal and poetic ambition. Each of those cases is limited by corpus size, translation dependence or the status of non-textual or hybrid work in a judgment of an oeuvre.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is translation. The achievement is bound up with dense Romanian wordplay, rhythm and syntactic patterning, and I cannot confirm how much of it survives in the translations available to a committee that reads largely in translation. A second concern is that recurrent motifs and enormous scale could read as insularity or self-repetition rather than deepening, and some of the longest books may be uneven in control. The poetry and early work are thinner in translation than the novels, so the whole-oeuvre claim is less well evidenced than the claim for the major novels. Finally, the opening rankings put Cărtărescu first in all six lists. That convergence is not literary evidence and should not shorten the scrutiny of these reservations.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Pierre Michon second for an exceptionally compressed, highly worked French prose whose voice is recognizable within a sentence. She argues that its intensity compensates for a small corpus, while accepting that compactness limits scale and that translation loses an uncertain amount.
responses.response: I agree that Michon's linguistic and formal achievement is among the highest on the list, and I ranked him fourth, not lower. A small oeuvre is not a defect in itself. But the criteria ask about sustained quality and significance across a body of work, and a compact corpus gives the committee less evidence of range and development. The loss in translation is also greatest where the achievement lies in syntax and cadence. I would keep him as a serious candidate for a later year. Intensity does not yet outweigh the breadth and development that the major Cărtărescu cycles demonstrate, and that case depends on the Romanian prose carrying over, which I have flagged as uncertain.

responses.point: Sward ranks Can Xue second and argues that her dream-logic fiction has few parallels. She treats the strangeness as a deliberate method with its own internal rigor, not an ornament, and sustained across a long career. She notes that the translated share of the output is limited.
responses.response: I accept that the estrangement is method and not ornament, and that the voice has few close parallels. That is why she is on the shortlist. I placed her last among my eight for reasons I think Sward partly shares. The translated corpus is a limited and possibly unrepresentative sample, and a style built on estrangement depends heavily on how translators handle it. It is also hard to tell from that sample whether the method deepens or repeats. I would want better evidence on development across the full Chinese-language output before weighing her against a writer whose development is easier to follow. I agree with Sward's own point that Cărtărescu's recent books suggest widening, not repetition, although I can only judge that from public knowledge.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Anne Carson second for remaking the boundaries between classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and visual form. She values the formal invention and linguistic precision, but notes that the genre-crossing and translation work make a citation within Nobel's will hard to articulate.
responses.response: I share both halves of this. Carson's invention is real and her engagement with antiquity is deep, which is why she is among my alternatives. But I think the difficulty Carlberg names is more than a drafting problem. Part of the effect of Nox lives in the book as an object, and the weight given to translation and scholarship is unsettled. A citation would have to define exactly what is being honored. Cărtărescu's case is more continuous across a body of poetry and prose, and so is easier to state for the whole oeuvre. I would keep Carson open as the English-language alternative if the committee concludes the Romanian prose cannot be adequately judged in translation.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first for voice and formal ambition. She notes that part of the appeal rests on immense scale and recurrent motifs, so repetitiveness is a concern, and that the poetry and early work are less accessible in translation.
responses.response: I take the repetitiveness concern seriously and think it is the real test of this candidacy. Recurrent motifs can be a unified imaginative world or a closed circuit, and the answer has to come from the books, not from their reputation. My own view, from public knowledge, is that the later large works show a project that deepens, but I have not read the texts and cannot settle it. Palm's point about uneven coverage of the poetry is also right, and it argues for a citation grounded mainly in the major prose works, with the poetry as a related strand.

uncertainties: Whether the translations available to the committee convey the patterning, wordplay and rhythm of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose well enough to support a whole-oeuvre judgment.
Whether recurrent motifs and very large scale in the late novels amount to deepening or to self-repetition.
How much of the poetry and early work is available in translation, and so how far the citation can responsibly cover it.
How to weigh Michon's compact corpus, and Zurita's and Carson's non-textual or hybrid strands, against a whole-oeuvre standard.
The translated corpus of Can Xue and Yan Lianke may not represent the full output, and a regional expert assessment would help.
My knowledge is from public reputation, not direct reading or independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and Celan is context only. The profile records no tie to any shortlisted writer, and my own practice is not evidence of a preference.
